questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presented with fevers and a swollen right eyelid with a red eye, purulent drainage, tearing, and some blurriness. She was normally well and did not take any regular medications. She had no known drug allergies. She reported contact with a person that had recent smallpox vaccination as he had just joined the military. On exam, she had periorbital edema and redness on the right eyelid with a cutaneous vesicle present. She had visual acuity of 20/40 on the right. There was no inflammation of the cornea. Right submandibular and preauricular lymphadenopathy were also present. Conjunctival scrapings were sent for microbiology.
questions.lead_in: What is the best treatment option?
questions.explanation: Vaccinia immunoglobulin and topical trifluridine The patient has vaccine-associated preseptal cellulitis and conjunctivitis from contact with the military recruit who had recent smallpox immunization. It is important to remember that patients who receive smallpox vaccination may shed live virus while the vaccination site is healing. This typically lasts until separation of the scab which is usually 2–3 weeks after the vaccination. Vaccinia immunoglobulin and topical trifluridine are the treatment of choice. More severe cases warrant immunoglobulin, and it does help decrease shedding of virus. While vancomycin and a cephalosporin would be reasonable for the preseptal cellulitis, it would not address the conjunctivitis in this case. The vesicle points toward a viral etiology. Azithromycin would be for suspected Chlamydia; however, the clinical scenario is not consistent with such given the vesicle and recent contact with a contact of a recently vaccinated person.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ophthalmoplegia (limited/absent extraocular movement) — in preseptal cellulitis movements are full and painless. (2) Proptosis (measure by exophthalmometry; ≥2 mm difference is significant) — absent in preseptal disease. (3) Deep eye pain and pain with eye movement, with decreased vision or an afferent pupillary defect — vision and pupil are normal in preseptal cellulitis.
b) (1) CN III (oculomotor): ptosis, dilated/poorly reactive pupil, eye deviated “down and out” with impaired adduction/elevation. (2) CN IV (trochlear): superior oblique palsy — impaired downward gaze in adduction, vertical diplopia/head tilt. (3) CN VI (abducens): lateral rectus palsy — failure of abduction, horizontal diplopia (often the earliest nerve involved). (4) CN V (V1 ± V2): decreased sensation over the forehead and sometimes the cheek. Bilateral cranial neuropathies are typical because the cavernous sinus is a venous plexus extending to the opposite side.

cohort_answer.text:
Three signs/symptoms: Ophthalmoplegia; Pain with eye movements; Proptosis; Diplopia. Orbital cellulitis: infection of contents of the orbit (fat and ocular muscles), distinguished from Preseptal cellulitis (sometimes called periorbital cellulitis): infection of the anterior portion of the eyelid. Neither infection involves the globe itself. Micro: Staph aureus, Strep pyogenes, H.flu, Fungi (mucorales, aspergillus), Mycobacteria (TB). Complications: Subperiosteal abscess; Orbital abscess; Epidural or subdural empyema; Brain abscess; Meningitis; Cavernous sinus thrombosis
Four nerves and clinical signs: CN III – Eye turned downward and outward. Ptosis. CN IV – Eye turned upwards and inwards. Limited adduction and intorsion (Superior oblique weakness). CN V – Loss of facial sensation. CN VI – Right eye turned medially. Inability to abduct eye (Lateral rectus weakness)

parts.text: 4 symptoms that point towards it being orbital cellulitis vs. preseptal cellulitis

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Proptosis (≥2 mm difference on exophthalmometry). (2) Ophthalmoplegia — limited extraocular movement. (3) Deep eye pain and pain on eye movement. (4) Decreased visual acuity, often with an afferent pupillary defect. In preseptal cellulitis vision is normal, there is no afferent pupillary defect, movements are full and painless, and there is no proptosis. Note fever and leukocytosis, usual in children, may be absent in adults (fever in only 30% of adult cases vs 70% pediatric).

questions.model_answer:
a) The orbital septum — a thin fibrous membrane arising from the orbital periosteum at the orbital rim and extending to the tarsal plates; infection anterior to it is preseptal, posterior to it is orbital.
b) (1) Proptosis: present in orbital, absent in preseptal. (2) Ophthalmoplegia: present in orbital, extraocular movements full in preseptal. (3) Pain with eye movement/deep eye pain: orbital only. (4) Visual acuity decreased ± afferent pupillary defect in orbital; vision normal and no APD in preseptal. (5) Extent of tissue involved: orbital cellulitis involves orbital soft tissue (fat, muscle) and is usually sinusitis-derived with risk of abscess/intracranial spread, whereas preseptal involves only the lids (CT shows lid edema without proptosis or orbital fat streaking).
c) The ethmoid sinus — separated from the orbit only by the paper-thin lamina papyracea, which has multiple foramina and sometimes natural defects (Zuckerkandl dehiscences); ethmoid sinusitis is the most common cause of sinus-related orbital infection and of subperiosteal abscess.
d) Septic cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis (CN VI palsy) — confirm with MRI/MRV.

questions.model_answer:
a) The orbital septum (fibrous membrane from orbital periosteum at the rim to the tarsal plates); anterior = preseptal, posterior = orbital.
b) (1) Proptosis. (2) Ophthalmoplegia. (3) Deep eye pain and pain on eye movement. (4) Decreased vision ± afferent pupillary defect. (5) Fever with leukocytosis (usual in children, present in only ~30% of adults). All of (1)-(4) are absent in preseptal cellulitis.
c) The ethmoid sinus. Its lateral wall is the paper-thin lamina papyracea, which is also the medial orbital wall; it carries multiple foramina for nerves and vessels and may have congenital Zuckerkandl dehiscences, so infection crosses readily beneath the periorbita as a subperiosteal abscess. Ethmoid sinusitis causes nearly all subperiosteal abscesses.
d) Septic cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis.

cohort_answer.text:
Anatomic landmark: The orbital septum - a thin, fibrous membrane arising from orbital periosteum, a barrier between the lids and the orbit. Infections anterior to the septum are preseptal (lid only), posterior to the septum are orbital (fat, muscles of orbit).
5 symptoms: Ophthalmoplegia (paralysis, absent in pre-septal); proptosis (absent in pre-septal); fever (more common in children); pain with eye movement; vision can be decreased (absent in pre-septal); afferent pupillary defect; leukocytosis (more common in children).
Highest risk sinus and why: Ethmoid. The orbit is surrounded by sinuses (frontal superiorly, maxillary inferiorly, ethmoid medially). The medial orbital wall is made from the lateral ethmoid sinus wall formed by a paper-thin lamina papyracea, contains multiple foramina for nerves/blood vessels, and some people have natural defects called Zuckerkandl dehiscences. For these anatomic reasons, ethmoid sinusitis is the most common cause of sinus-related orbital infection.
Ipsilateral eye palsy diagnosis: Septic cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis. The venous drainage of the eye and face is through the cavernous sinus, risk for cavernous venous sinus syndrome; the cavernous sinus is a venous plexus extending to the opposite side, allowing spread of infection with bilateral cranial neuropathies typical. Suspect this diagnosis with involvement of CN III, IV, VI, V2 (maxillary) branch, or bilateral involvement of cranial neuropathies.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Proptosis. (2) Ophthalmoplegia with pain on extraocular movement. (3) Decreased visual acuity or afferent pupillary defect. (Chemosis and marked lid swelling also favour orbital involvement.)
b) CN III (oculomotor): ptosis, dilated/nonreactive pupil, eye deviated down and out, impaired adduction/elevation. CN IV (trochlear): superior oblique palsy — impaired depression of the adducted eye, vertical diplopia, compensatory head tilt. CN V (trigeminal, V1 ± V2): decreased sensation over the forehead and sometimes cheek (seen in ~25% of cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis, not typical of plain orbital cellulitis). CN VI (abducens): lateral rectus palsy — failure of abduction, esotropia, horizontal diplopia. Bilateral cranial neuropathies are typical, and contralateral orbital signs usually appear within 24-48 hours.

B) III (oculomotor): Downward (SO4), outward gaze (LR6), dilated pupil. IV (trochlear): Hypertropia, head tilt. V (trigeminal): Deviation of the jaw, paresthesias, pain, inability to chew or bite down. VI (abducens): esotropia.

questions.model_answer:
a) Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group — the most common isolate in pediatric sinogenic orbital infection (44% of culture-positive cases); Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA; group A streptococci; Streptococcus pneumoniae; Haemophilus influenzae (including nontypeable); anaerobes such as Fusobacterium and Eikenella (~14%); gram-negative bacilli.
b) Prompt IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering S. aureus/MRSA, streptococci including S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and other gram-negative bacilli, and anaerobes, with good CNS penetration — e.g. IV vancomycin + metronidazole + ceftriaxone. Add antipseudomonal coverage if immunocompromised, known Pseudomonas sinus colonization, or recent multiple antibiotics. Tailor to culture results. Monitor closely for visual compromise; surgical drainage for orbital abscess (nearly always) and for subperiosteal abscess in older children/large (>10 mm) abscesses — young children with small medial subperiosteal abscesses often respond to IV antibiotics alone with close follow-up.
c) CBC with differential and blood cultures in all cases; sinus cultures if sinusitis and abscess drainage cultures; nasal MRSA screening; contrast CT of the orbits and sinuses in any patient with orbital signs (proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, decreased vision) to identify a drainable abscess, repeated if failing IV therapy; MRI/MRV if cavernous sinus thrombosis suspected; ophthalmology and ENT involvement.

cohort_answer.text:
Group A Streptococcus; S. aureus (including MRSA); S. pneumoniae; H. influenzae; Moraxella; S. anginosus; Oral anaerobes
CTX + Flagyl +/- Clox or Vanco. (UTD: Vanco + CTX/Cefotaxime + metronidazole for anaerobic coverage until intracranial involvement excluded; fluoroquinolone + vanco if penicillin/cephalosporin allergic)
BCx; CT Head+Orbits (consider MRI in kids due to radiation); consider LP if suspecting meningitis; ENT/Ophtho consult +/- neurosurgery and plastics

questions.model_answer:
a) The orbital septum — a thin fibrous membrane from the orbital periosteum at the rim to the tarsal plates; infection anterior to it is preseptal (lids only), posterior to it is orbital (fat and muscle within the bony orbit).
b) (1) Proptosis. (2) Ophthalmoplegia. (3) Pain on extraocular movement/deep eye pain. (4) Diplopia. (5) Decreased visual acuity with afferent pupillary defect (chemosis also supports orbital involvement).
c) The ethmoid sinus: its lateral wall is the paper-thin lamina papyracea, which forms the medial orbital wall, contains multiple foramina for nerves and vessels, and may have natural Zuckerkandl dehiscences — so infection readily crosses to collect beneath the medial periorbita. d) Septic cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis — suspect it with CN VI palsy, contralateral orbital signs within 24-48 hours, or bilateral CN III/IV/VI neuropathies ± V1/V2 sensory loss; image with MRI/MRV.

cohort_answer.text: Anatomic structure: Orbital septum - thin fibrous membrane serving as barrier between superficial lids and orbit; infections anterior to septum are preseptal, posterior are orbital (Mandell's); preseptal involves only lids not the orbit, orbital cellulitis involves soft tissues (fat, muscle) within bony orbit. Signs of orbital cellulitis: Proptosis; Painful extraocular eye movement; Ophthalmoplegia; Diplopia; Chemosis. Highest risk sinus: Ethmoid - separated from orbit by thin lamina papyracea (medial wall of orbit), contains multiple foramina for nerves/vessels, some people have natural defects; nearly all periosteal abscesses secondary to ethmoid sinusitis. Complication to rule out with cranial nerve palsy: Cavernous sinus thrombosis - spread to opposite eye through cavernous sinus usually within 24-48 hours of initial unilateral orbital findings; may present with bilateral findings or signs of bilateral neuropathies of CN III, IV, VI without lid edema/erythema typical of orbital cellulitis, especially from skin infections of middle third of face or dental infections
